This page covers the exact US occupation O*NET/SOC 15-1211.01, "Health Informatics Specialists": applying nursing and informatics knowledge to assist in the design, development, and ongoing modification of computerized healthcare systems; they may train staff and assist with problem-solving to support system implementation. Original official scope: Apply knowledge of nursing and informatics to assist in the design, development, and ongoing modification of computerized health care systems. May educate staff and assist in problem solving to promote the implementation of the health care system. Core tasks listed by O*NET include translating nursing practice information between nurses and systems engineers, analysts, or designers (importance: 95); applying informatics knowledge to design or implement health information technology applications to solve clinical or healthcare administrative problems (93); developing or implementing policies or practices to ensure patient information privacy, confidentiality, or security (86); analyzing and interpreting patient, nursing, or information system data to improve nursing services (83); identifying, collecting, recording, or analyzing patient care data (81); collaborating with other health informatics specialists to apply computer science, information science, nursing, and informatics theories to nursing practice, education, administration, or research (80); developing, implementing, or evaluating health information technology applications, tools, processes, or structures to assist nurses with data management (79); designing, developing, selecting, testing, implementing, and evaluating new or modified informatics solutions, data structures, and decision support mechanisms to support patients, healthcare professionals, their information management, and interactions among people, computers, and technology (79); disseminating nursing informatics science and practice information to the profession, other healthcare professions, nursing students, and the public (75); analyzing computer and information technologies for applicability to nursing practice, education, administration, and research (73); developing strategies, policies, or procedures for introducing, evaluating, or modifying information technology applied to nursing practice, administration, education, or research (70); reading current literature, communicating with colleagues, and participating in professional organizations or conferences to keep up with informatics developments (68); developing or providing health information technology training programs and preparing operating manuals as needed (68); designing, conducting, or supporting nursing informatics research (68); informing local, state, national, and international health policy on information management and communication, confidentiality and security, patient safety, infrastructure development, and economics (67); advising nurses on hardware or software configuration (61); and planning, installing, repairing, or troubleshooting telehealth technology applications or systems in homes (44). Common titles include Clinical Electronic Health Record Nurse, Clinical Informaticist, Clinical Informatics Analyst, Clinical Informatics Nurse, Clinical Informatics Specialist, Health Informaticist, Nursing Informatics Officer, Nursing Informatics Specialist, RN Clinical Information Systems Coordinator, and RN Clinical Information Systems Educator. Practice scenario | An entirely fictional healthcare information system implementation task package (for practicing the process only; it represents no real organization, system, patient, data, or vendor). Draft a plan addressing: (1) how to organize a health informatics implementation plan using fictional clinical workflows, requirements, and information system design documents, with a structured approach covering users, clinical needs and workflow identification; data, information standards and sources; system design, configuration and decision support; privacy, security and access control; training, go-live and changes; monitoring, evaluation and improvement; and ethics, compliance and informed-consent boundaries. Specify information gaps requiring supplementation, including clinical workflows and user roles; data and terminology standards and mappings; system interfaces, availability and performance; privacy, security and access control requirements; training, change management and rollback plans; and evaluation indicators and acceptance criteria. (2) How to design completion and review points for a fictional system implementation and monitoring record form, covering fields and definitions; users, roles and permissions; configurations, versions and changes; interfaces, data mappings and validation; anomalies, defects and handling; and go-live, rollback and traceability. (3) How to write a system implementation description suitable for handover: requirements and goals—design standards and data mappings—configuration and changes—privacy and security—training and go-live—monitoring, evaluation and outstanding items. (4) How to record and retain system configuration, change, defect, user, and patient-related data, distinguishing disclosable information from controlled materials or those involving patient health information and protected health information. (5) How to pause, review, and escalate when requirements are unclear or data do not conform to standards, systems deviate from clinical and compliance requirements, security or privacy risks arise, clinical judgment or medical advice is involved, or the role's authorization is exceeded. Use public materials and simulated data; do not use real patient data or personal health information.

Fit signals | US O*NET 15-1211.01 work activity importance scores identify working with computers (94), getting information (92), making decisions and solving problems (89), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (88), interpreting the meaning of information for others (88), analyzing data or information (87), establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships (86), organizing, planning, and prioritizing work (85), updating and using relevant knowledge (85), developing teams (83), thinking creatively (82), evaluating information to determine compliance with standards (81), and processing information (81) as this occupation's most important activities. Work context data (response percentages) show email every day for 100%, working indoors in environmentally controlled conditions every day for 86%, telephone conversations every day for 81%, face-to-face discussions every day for 65%, working with or contributing to a work group or team extremely important for 85%, constant contact with others for 48%, being exact or accurate extremely important for 55%, some freedom to determine tasks, priorities, and goals for 71%, working more than 40 hours per week for 52%, sitting more than half the time for 57%, and some freedom to make decisions for 67%. If you are willing to translate clinical and business requirements into implementable information system plans, communicate with clinical, engineering, and compliance stakeholders, and accept responsibility for system quality and patient information privacy and security, this occupation's daily requirements may align more closely with your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (15-1211.01, work activity importance scores and work context response percentages) working with computers (94), getting information (92), making decisions and solving problems (89), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (88), interpreting the meaning of information for others (88), and analyzing data or information (87) as the highest activities. Contact with others is constant for 48%; being exact or accurate is extremely important for 55% and very important for 25%; consequences of error are extremely serious for 19%, very serious for 14%, serious for 19%, and fairly serious for 33%; responsibility for work outcomes and others' results is very high for 35% and high for 25%; time pressure occurs at least monthly for 43%; and repeating the same tasks is very important for 33%. This occupation focuses on nursing, clinical practice, informatics, and information system design, implementation, and ongoing modification. Errors in translating requirements, data, or standards; undocumented system configurations or changes; inappropriate access control, privacy, or security settings; statements crossing into clinical judgment or medical advice; or improper patient information processing or disclosure can damage clinical workflows and create patient safety, compliance, and legal risks. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed, SVP 8.0 and above). The education section shows a master's degree for 52%, a bachelor's degree for 19%, and a post-baccalaureate certificate for 10%. The occupation usually requires understanding both clinical work and information systems, creating substantial demands for cross-disciplinary communication and responsibility. If you find it difficult to sustain communication with clinical, engineering, and compliance stakeholders, bear responsibility for patient information and system security and consequences of error, or accept responsibility for the integrity of requirements, data, and privacy compliance, treat these as practical costs requiring careful consideration.

Taking responsibility for judgment | Real fit depends on whether you can accomplish three things together in the same health informatics assignment: do the professional work thoroughly (design, implement, evaluate, and continually modify systems using clinical workflows, requirements, data, and information standards, cite practices consistent with current standards and specifications, and produce usable design, configuration, change, and monitoring records); manage compliance, privacy, and boundaries (work and keep records under medical information privacy, security, informed-consent, and data protection requirements; distinguish disclosable information from controlled materials or those involving patient health information and protected health information and handle them under established rules; and avoid crossing into clinical judgment, medical diagnosis, or medication advice); and accept clearly defined job responsibilities (be accountable for your requirements translation, system design, configuration, changes, monitoring, and records, and refer matters beyond authorization or involving clinical judgment, medical advice, and external disclosure to the appropriate roles or organizations under established rules). Test this through a verifiable experience, such as completing a health informatics implementation plan and implementation and monitoring recordkeeping notes for a fictional task, or reviewing the handling of a system defect or security and privacy risk, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire's conclusion.

Direct answer | The health informatics specialists covered here are the exact occupation O*NET 15-1211.01 (Health Informatics Specialists). Their work falls into several categories: (I) Requirements and clinical workflow translation—translate nursing and clinical practice information between nurses and systems engineers, analysts, or designers (importance: 95) and identify clinical and business requirements and workflows. (II) System, data, and standards design—apply informatics knowledge to design or implement health information technology applications to solve clinical or administrative problems (93); design, develop, select, test, and implement new or modified informatics solutions, data structures, and decision support mechanisms (79). (III) Privacy, security, and compliance—develop or implement policies or practices ensuring patient information privacy, confidentiality, or security (86) and inform health policy on information management, confidentiality, and security (67). (IV) Data and evaluation—analyze and interpret patient, nursing, or information system data to improve nursing services (83) and identify, collect, record, or analyze patient care data (81). (V) Training, support, and dissemination—develop or provide health information technology training and prepare operating manuals as needed (68), advise nurses on hardware or software configuration (61), and disseminate nursing informatics knowledge and practice to the profession, other healthcare professions, nursing students, and the public (75). (VI) Research and ongoing modification—design, conduct, or support nursing informatics research (68), develop strategies, policies, or procedures for introducing, evaluating, or modifying information technology (70), and read literature and participate in professional organizations to keep up with developments (68). The work cycle connects requirements and workflow translation—system, data, and standards design—privacy, security, and compliance—data and evaluation—training, support, and dissemination—research, ongoing modification, and review. This page does not conflate this occupation with adjacent clinical data managers, clinical research coordinators, computer systems analysts, health education specialists, health information technologists and medical registrars, medical and health services managers, nurse practitioners, patient representatives, or social science research assistants. Nor does it expand health informatics responsibilities to replace clinical diagnosis, treatment, medication, or medical decisions.

Mainland China scope and gaps | Mainland China has roles similar to health informatics specialists in healthcare informatization, hospital information, nursing informatization, health information management, and healthcare big data, such as hospital information department engineers, health information and medical record information professionals, clinical and nursing informatics staff, and healthcare big data and data governance personnel. Their work, qualifications, standards, and records are governed by the Law of the People's Republic of China on Basic Medical and Health Care and the Promotion of Health, Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China, Data Security Law of the People's Republic of China, Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China, and specifications related to healthcare organization informatization, electronic medical records, and network and data security. Medical information system construction and operation must follow standards and specifications; diagnosis, treatment, and medication must be handled by appropriately qualified organizations and personnel; and patient health information and personal health information must be legally protected and processed on a minimum-necessary basis. However, this round did not obtain a nationwide occupational wage distribution exactly corresponding to US O*NET 15-1211.01 (Health Informatics Specialists). The National Bureau of Statistics publishes average wages of persons employed in urban units by industry category, an industry-level scope without occupational distinctions or a separate listing for this occupation. Under the evidence policy, this page records only statistical scopes and visible gaps (marked "Insufficient evidence:"), without using industry averages, advertised recruitment pay, or US wages to extrapolate starting salaries, medians, or individual income across jurisdictions. The Chinese and US scopes differ in legal environments and statistical periods; they are neither combined nor converted.

Ethics and privacy notes | Organize work under medical information privacy, security, and data protection requirements. Systems, data, and materials must align with current standards and specifications and identify sources and limitations; they must not replace clinical diagnosis, treatment, medication, or medical advice. Patient and user data must follow the principles of keeping data subjects informed, minimum necessity, purpose limitation, and de-identification. Patient health information or protected health information must be accessed, stored, and shared under organizational and legal requirements. Access control, auditing, encryption, and backups must follow information security requirements. System changes and go-live require necessary approval and testing. Immediately pause and escalate for review under established rules when requirements are unclear or data do not conform to standards, systems deviate from clinical and compliance requirements, security or privacy risks arise, or clinical advice or matters beyond authorization are involved. This page does not constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, legal, or compliance advice.

Standards and quality boundaries | This page involves three types of requirements. Professional practice and quality: requirements translation, system design, data mapping, and evaluation must follow clinical workflows and current information standards and specifications, with configuration, change, and monitoring records maintained. Ethics, privacy, and security: systems must follow minimum necessity, purpose limitation, access control, and auditing; patient health information or protected health information must be managed under organizational and legal requirements; and clinical judgment, diagnosis, or medication advice must not be provided beyond the role's scope. Records and information: configuration, change, defect, acceptance, and user records must be truthful, complete, and traceable. Controlled materials or those involving patient health information, as well as externally disclosed information, must be managed through approval and minimum necessity. This page offers general reminders only and does not constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, legal, or compliance advice.

Records and collaboration | Under organizational informatization, information security, and data management rules, record users, roles and permissions; requirements, workflows and data mappings; configurations, versions and changes; interfaces, validation and performance; anomalies, defects and handling; training, go-live and rollback; acceptance, monitoring and evaluation; and original records and revision trails, using prescribed templates and deadlines. Immediately pause when requirements are unclear or data do not conform to standards, systems deviate from clinical and compliance requirements, security or privacy risks arise, or records differ from site conditions. Escalate within your authorization and request review by compliance, information security, and clinical roles. Do not modify records or add entries retrospectively on your own authority.

Boundary conclusion | This page covers O*NET 15-1211.01 (Health Informatics Specialists). The core differences from adjacent roles lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority. This occupation focuses on clinical and business requirements and health information system design, implementation, and ongoing modification, producing design, configuration, change, and monitoring records according to clinical requirements and data and information standards. Clinical Data Managers (15-2051.02) focus on clinical research data management; Clinical Research Coordinators (11-9121.01) on clinical research project coordination; Computer Systems Analysts (15-1211.00) on general information system analysis and design; Health Education Specialists (21-1091.00) on health education and promotion programs; Health Information Technologists and Medical Registrars (29-9021.00) on medical records, medical registries, and health information technical support; Medical and Health Services Managers (11-9111.00) on healthcare service operations management; Nurse Practitioners (29-1171.00) on clinical diagnosis, treatment, and nursing care; Patient Representatives (29-2099.08) on patient communication and rights assistance; and Social Science Research Assistants (19-4061.00) on social science research assistance. Their subjects, outputs, and levels of authority differ. Authority for clinical judgment, medical advice, system go-live, and disclosure cannot be carried across roles.

Core principles of adjacent roles | Most roles in the same group and adjacent roles aim to bring clinical needs, data, systems, research, or services to a prescribed condition within standards, compliance, and authorization boundaries while maintaining records. Their differences lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority: some focus on health information system design and implementation, others on clinical research data, general information systems, health education programs, medical records and registries, healthcare operations, clinical diagnosis and treatment, patient assistance, or research assistance.

This occupation's core purpose | Working with clinical and business requirements, data, information standards, and information systems, complete work within standards, compliance, and authorization limits: requirements and workflow translation, system, data and standards design, privacy, security and compliance, data and evaluation, training, support and dissemination, and research, ongoing modification and review. This enables accurate translation of clinical requirements, traceability of system quality, configurations and changes, control of patient information privacy and security, and clear responsibility boundaries.

Main subjects and bases of adjacent roles | Clinical data managers follow clinical research data management and quality standards; clinical research coordinators follow clinical research standards and regulations; computer systems analysts use general information system analysis and software engineering methods; health education specialists follow public health and health education specifications; health information technologists and medical registrars follow medical record, medical registry, and health information management specifications; medical and health services managers follow healthcare service operations and management specifications; nurse practitioners follow clinical diagnosis, treatment, and nursing specifications; patient representatives follow patient service and rights assistance specifications; and social science research assistants use social science research methods and ethical standards.

This occupation's main subjects and basis | Subjects include clinical and business requirements and workflows; data and terminology standards and mappings; system design, configuration and changes; privacy, security and access control; training, go-live and rollback; and evaluation, monitoring and improvement. The basis is healthcare informatization, information security, data protection, and medical information privacy specifications and organizational project, change, and data rules.

Occupational profile | The health informatics specialists covered here are the exact occupation O*NET 15-1211.01 (Health Informatics Specialists). In healthcare organizations, informatization vendors, health information, and health technology settings, they translate clinical and business requirements and design, implement, and continually modify health information systems. They translate nursing and clinical practice information between nurses and systems engineers, analysts, or designers; apply informatics knowledge to design or implement health information technology applications; develop or implement patient information privacy and security policies; analyze and interpret clinical and information system data; design and test informatics solutions, data structures, and decision support mechanisms; develop or provide training; disseminate nursing informatics knowledge to professionals and the public; and support research. Common titles include Clinical Electronic Health Record Nurse, Clinical Informaticist, Clinical Informatics Analyst, Clinical Informatics Nurse, Clinical Informatics Specialist, Health Informaticist, and Nursing Informatics Specialist. O*NET's 15-1211.01 page shows the main US industries (parent occupation 15-1211.00 scope) as professional, scientific, and technical services and finance and insurance. The highest work activities are working with computers (importance: 94), getting information (92), making decisions and solving problems (89), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (88), and interpreting the meaning of information for others (88). Email is used every day for 100%, work indoors in environmentally controlled conditions occurs every day for 86%, and telephone conversations occur every day for 81%; being exact or accurate is extremely important for 55%; consequences of error are extremely serious for 19%, very serious for 14%, serious for 19%, and fairly serious for 33%. O*NET places the occupation in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed, SVP 8.0 and above). The education section shows a master's degree for 52%, a bachelor's degree for 19%, and a post-baccalaureate certificate for 10%. Each step must be documented under informatization, information security, and data rules and be reviewable by supervisors, compliance, and clinical roles.

Main outputs of adjacent roles | Clinical data managers produce clinical research data and quality records; clinical research coordinators produce study coordination and compliance records; computer systems analysts produce business requirements and system design documents; health education specialists produce needs assessments, program plans, and evaluation records; health information technologists and medical registrars produce medical record coding, registry, and system operation records; medical and health services managers produce operations, budget, and staffing documents; nurse practitioners produce clinical assessment, diagnosis, treatment, and nursing records; patient representatives produce patient communication and assistance records; and social science research assistants produce research data and assistance records.

This occupation's main outputs | Requirements and workflow translation notes completed according to clinical requirements and data and information standards; system design, configuration, data structure and decision support records; privacy, security, access control and audit configuration records; interface, data mapping and validation records; training, go-live and rollback records; monitoring, evaluation, defect and change records; and traceable compliance, data protection, and verification records.

Responsible parties in adjacent roles | Responsibilities in the same group and adjacent roles are usually defined by their organizations, professions, compliance requirements, and standards. The subjects of responsibility commonly include clinical and business users, patient information, system security, and organizational compliance.

Professionals in this occupation are responsible for the requirements translation, system design, configuration, changes, monitoring, evaluation, and records they perform and sign, and for work and conclusions completed according to clinical requirements, specifications, information security, and data rules. Clinical judgment, diagnosis, treatment, medication, medical advice, system go-live and external disclosure, and patient health information processing and disclosure are decided under established rules by appropriately qualified roles or organizations; this occupation does not replace their decisions.

Authority and approval in adjacent roles | Authority in the same group and adjacent roles comes from organizational authorization, professional practice, compliance, and standards. It usually does not include independent authority to decide conclusions, signatures, or release approvals beyond one's authorization or scope. Clinical decisions, major changes, disclosure, and go-live decisions should be referred to the appropriate roles or organizations.

This occupation's authority and approval | Routine requirements translation, system design, configuration, changes, training, and monitoring must remain within specifications and organizational authorization. Clinical judgment, medical advice, external disclosure, and patient health information processing and disclosure must follow qualification and approval requirements. System go-live and major changes must receive approval from the relevant roles or organizations under established rules or be referred to them. Do not make judgments or grant release approval beyond your authority.

Limits of conclusions in adjacent roles | Conclusions in the same group and adjacent roles are mostly limited to the project and responsibilities concerned and usually do not constitute determinations of clinical outcomes, medical diagnoses, legal liability, or system security. Cross-disciplinary conclusions and those involving clinical matters, major changes, and disclosure have limits on their applicability.

This occupation's conclusion boundaries | System, data, and evaluation conclusions state only verifiable requirements, configuration, change, validation, monitoring, and evaluation records, distinguishing measured facts, judgments and inferences, and matters awaiting verification. Do not make unauthorized judgments or commitments on matters beyond your authority (clinical judgment, medical advice, system go-live and external disclosure, and patient health information processing and disclosure). If requirements are unclear or data do not conform to standards, systems deviate from clinical and compliance requirements, security or privacy risks arise, or records differ from site conditions, pause and escalate or hand over. Conclusions must also withstand review by supervisors, compliance, information security and clinical roles, and regulatory inspections.

Pre-employment verification notes | The following six items are for checking individually before applying for or starting a job, to avoid inferring actual responsibilities and authority from titles or promotional language. Verification should be based on written recruitment information, employment contracts, job descriptions, and informatization, information security, and data policy documents, and should continue after joining. This page lists areas to check, not a formal requirements checklist for any organization or role. Special note: US O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed, SVP 8.0 and above). In mainland China, hospital informatization, health information, and data governance roles often have professional and continuing education requirements. Confirm the role's specific requirements for education, training, certification, continuing education, patient health information processing, and role authorization.

Verification notes | Similar titles can carry very different responsibilities and authority. Some focus on translating clinical and nursing informatics requirements and designing systems, others on health data governance, standards and data quality, electronic medical records and system operations, maintenance and support, clinical research data management, or general information system analysis and development. Organizations and jurisdictions also differ in their authorization for clinical advice, data and privacy, system go-live, and external disclosure.

paragraphs: Conclusion | The core differences between this occupation (O*NET 15-1211.01, Health Informatics Specialists) and adjacent roles lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority. This occupation focuses on clinical and business requirements and health information system design, implementation, and ongoing modification, producing design, configuration, change, and monitoring records according to clinical requirements and data and information standards. Health Information Technologists and Medical Registrars (29-9021.00) focus on medical records, medical registries, and health information technical support; Clinical Data Managers (15-2051.02) on clinical research data management; Computer Systems Analysts (15-1211.00) on general information system analysis and design; Clinical Research Coordinators (11-9121.01) on clinical research project coordination; and Medical and Health Services Managers (11-9111.00) on healthcare service operations management. Their subjects, outputs, and levels of authority differ. Authority for clinical judgment, medical advice, system go-live, and disclosure cannot be carried across roles.

Evidence note | The occupations compared below come from O*NET occupational classifications and public materials to help distinguish adjacent occupations' work and assess selection fit. They do not establish qualification, hiring, or pay conclusions, nor constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, legal, or compliance advice. Each occupation's wages and employment must be checked separately under its own SOC scope. This table makes no numerical comparison and does not use one occupation's wages as a proxy for another. Qualification, compliance, and data requirements must be checked under each jurisdiction's and organization's requirements. US wage and employment data on this page use the parent occupation 15-1211.00 (Computer Systems Analysts) scope explicitly identified by O*NET on its 15-1211.01 page. This page faithfully labels them as parent-occupation data rather than this exact occupation's own scope and does not borrow other adjacent occupations' figures.

Introduction | The following comparison uses four columns: career track—core work and outputs—key differences—which choice is a better fit. Health information systems, clinical data, medical records and registries, and healthcare operations often connect within the same healthcare organization or informatization vendor, but connection does not imply interchangeability. When moving between tracks, learn the new track's subjects, standards, data, authorization, and responsibility boundaries.

Key differences: this occupation focuses on clinical and business requirements and health information system design, implementation, and ongoing modification. It uses nursing and informatics knowledge to design, implement, and evaluate systems and provide configurations and plans within compliance and authorization limits, taking responsibility for system quality, data, privacy, and records. Other roles center on medical records, registries and health information technical support, clinical research data management, general information system analysis and design, clinical research coordination, or healthcare service operations management. They usually have more specialized standards, authorization, and subjects and do not bear primary responsibility for health information system design and implementation (but must collaborate with this occupation and clarify boundaries).

Better suited to people willing to translate clinical and business requirements into information system plans, communicate with clinical, engineering, and compliance stakeholders, and accept responsibility for system quality and patient information privacy and security.

Core work and outputs: translate nursing and clinical practice information between nurses and systems engineers, analysts, or designers; apply informatics knowledge to design or implement health information technology applications; develop or implement patient information privacy and security policies; analyze and interpret clinical and information system data; design and test informatics solutions, data structures, and decision support mechanisms; develop or provide training; disseminate nursing informatics knowledge to professionals and the public; and support research. Outputs are design, configuration, change, and monitoring records completed according to clinical requirements and data and information standards (O*NET/SOC 15-1211.01).
This occupation: Health Informatics Specialists (O*NET/SOC 15-1211.01)

Key differences: health information technologists and medical registrars focus on medical record coding, medical registries, and health information technical support, producing medical record, registry, and system operation records. This occupation focuses on translating clinical and business requirements and designing, implementing, and continually modifying health information systems, producing system design, configuration, and change records. Medical record coding and registry work are usually not its main duties (but it must collaborate with health information technologists and registrars to ensure accurate data).

Better suited to people who want to work with medical records, medical registries, and information system operational support; this occupation emphasizes clinical requirements translation, system design, implementation, and evaluation.

Core work and outputs: perform and record coding, registration, and information technology support under medical record, medical registry, and health information management specifications. Outputs are medical record, registry, and system operation records.
Health Information Technologists and Medical Registrars (29-9021.00)

Key differences: clinical data managers focus on clinical research data management and quality control, producing clinical research data and quality records. This occupation focuses on clinical and business requirements translation and health information systems, producing system design and configuration records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for clinical research data management (but must collaborate with clinical data managers to ensure consistent data standards).

Better suited to people who want to collect, clean, and control the quality of clinical research data and collaborate on statistics; this occupation emphasizes clinical requirements translation and system design and implementation.

Core work and outputs: collect, clean, and validate study data under clinical research data management and quality standards and support statistics and reports. Outputs are clinical research data and quality records.
Clinical Data Managers (15-2051.02)

Key differences: computer systems analysts focus on general business information system analysis and design, producing business requirements and system design documents. This occupation focuses on clinical and nursing settings and health information systems, producing clinical requirements translation, system design, and configuration records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for general business system analysis and development (although their requirements analysis and system design methods are closely related).

Better suited to people who want to analyze and design general business information systems; this occupation emphasizes clinical and nursing requirements translation and health information system design and implementation.

Core work and outputs: analyze general business requirements, design information systems, processes, and data plans, and support implementation. Outputs are business requirements and system design documents.
Computer Systems Analysts (15-1211.00)

Key differences: clinical research coordinators focus on study coordination, participant management, and compliance, producing study coordination and compliance records. This occupation focuses on clinical and business requirements translation and health information systems, producing system design and configuration records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for study coordination and participant management (but must collaborate with clinical research coordinators to support requirements and compliance for research-related systems).

Better suited to people who want to coordinate clinical research, manage participants, and handle compliance; this occupation emphasizes clinical requirements translation and system design and implementation.

Core work and outputs: coordinate studies, participant recruitment and follow-up, and compliance documents under clinical research specifications, maintaining records. Outputs are study coordination and compliance records.
Clinical Research Coordinators (11-9121.01)

Key differences: medical and health services managers focus on healthcare service operations, staffing, and budgets, producing operations, budget, and staffing documents. This occupation focuses on clinical and business requirements translation and health information systems, producing system design and configuration records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for departmental operations, staffing, and budget management (but must collaborate with medical and health services managers to align business goals and resources).
Better suited to people who want to manage healthcare service operations, staffing, and budgets; this occupation emphasizes clinical requirements translation and system design and implementation.

Core work and outputs: develop operations, staffing, and budget plans under healthcare service operations and management specifications and coordinate cross-departmental implementation. Outputs are operations, budget, and staffing documents.
Medical and Health Services Managers (11-9111.00)

Transition | This page places adjacent roles side by side by subjects, outputs, and levels of authority to help you decide which health information system, clinical data, medical record and registry, or healthcare operations roles you want to pursue over time. In any track, readiness to work depends on understanding its subjects, standards, data, and authorization requirements; clearly documenting requirements, designs or data, and records; and willingness to accept responsibility for patient information and compliance. Interest questionnaires only help raise questions.

Direct answer | The core occupational risk is not merely whether a system can go live, but four types of failure with serious consequences. Clinical and information failure: incorrect requirements translation, data and standard mapping, or system configuration can create mismatch between systems and clinical workflows; statements crossing into clinical judgment, diagnosis, or medication can damage clinical workflows and create patient safety risks. Privacy and security failure: inadequate minimum necessity, access control, or processing of patient health information or protected health information, insufficient de-identification, or sharing beyond permitted boundaries may cause patient information breaches and compliance and legal risks. Quality and evaluation failure: inadequate system design, configuration, changes, or testing, or inaccurate records may cause system failures, data quality and performance misjudgments, and patient risks. Authorization and collaboration failure: independently making clinical judgments, giving medical advice, approving system go-live, or disclosing externally beyond authorization; single-point dependence for critical certifications or system capabilities; and unclear standards with clinical, engineering, and vendor stakeholders on scope, responsibility, and disclosure boundaries can cause disputes. Work context data—constant contact with others for 48%, being exact or accurate extremely important for 55%, very high responsibility for work outcomes and others' results for 35%, and consequences of error that are extremely serious for 19%, very serious for 14%, serious for 19%, and fairly serious for 33%—provide context for the seriousness of these consequences.

entries.answer: The health informatics specialists covered here are the exact occupation O*NET 15-1211.01 (Health Informatics Specialists): applying nursing and informatics knowledge to assist in the design, development, and ongoing modification of computerized healthcare systems; they may train staff and assist with problem-solving to support system implementation. Core tasks include translating nursing practice information between nurses and systems engineers, analysts, or designers (importance: 95); applying informatics knowledge to design or implement health information technology applications (93); developing or implementing policies or practices ensuring patient information privacy, confidentiality, or security (86); analyzing and interpreting patient, nursing, or information system data to improve nursing services (83); identifying, collecting, recording, or analyzing patient care data (81); applying computer science, information science, nursing, and informatics theories to nursing practice (80); developing, implementing, or evaluating applications that assist nurses with data management (79); and designing and testing informatics solutions, data structures, and decision support mechanisms (79). Common titles include Clinical Electronic Health Record Nurse, Clinical Informaticist, Clinical Informatics Analyst, Clinical Informatics Nurse, Clinical Informatics Specialist, Health Informaticist, and Nursing Informatics Specialist. entries.answer: The core differences lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority. This occupation focuses on clinical and business requirements and health information system design, implementation, and ongoing modification, producing design, configuration, change, and monitoring records according to clinical requirements and data and information standards. Health Information Technologists and Medical Registrars (29-9021.00) focus on medical records, medical registries, and health information technical support; Clinical Data Managers (15-2051.02) on clinical research data management; Computer Systems Analysts (15-1211.00) on general information system analysis and design; Clinical Research Coordinators (11-9121.01) on clinical study coordination; Medical and Health Services Managers (11-9111.00) on healthcare service operations management; Health Education Specialists (21-1091.00) on health education and promotion programs; and Nurse Practitioners (29-1171.00) and Patient Representatives (29-2099.08) on clinical diagnosis and treatment and patient assistance. Their subjects, activities, and levels of authority differ. Authority for clinical judgment, medical advice, system go-live, and disclosure cannot be carried across roles.

subject.name: Health Informatics Specialists
subject.summary: Health informatics specialists correspond to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 15-1211.01, "Health Informatics Specialists": applying nursing and informatics knowledge to assist in the design, development, and ongoing modification of computerized healthcare systems; they may train staff and help solve problems to support system implementation. Core tasks include translating nursing and clinical practice information between nurses and systems engineers, analysts, or designers; applying informatics knowledge to design or implement health information technology applications; developing or implementing patient information privacy and security policies; analyzing and interpreting clinical and information system data; designing and testing informatics solutions, data structures, and decision support mechanisms; providing training, disseminating nursing informatics knowledge to professionals and the public, and supporting research. Common titles include Clinical Electronic Health Record Nurse, Clinical Informaticist, Clinical Informatics Analyst, Clinical Informatics Specialist, Health Informaticist, and Nursing Informatics Specialist. Original official scope: Apply knowledge of nursing and informatics to assist in the design, development, and ongoing modification of computerized health care systems. May educate staff and assist in problem solving to promote the implementation of the health care system. Scope note: O*NET explicitly labels the US wage, employment, and industry data presented on its 15-1211.01 page as covering Computer Systems Analysts (parent occupation 15-1211.00). This page faithfully labels them as parent-occupation data, never as this exact occupation's own scope (15-1211.01), and does not substitute adjacent occupations' figures. Projected growth for this occupation in 2024–2034 is 7% or higher, with a Bright Outlook designation, and O*NET places it in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed, SVP 8.0 and above). This page does not constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, legal, or compliance advice.
